intro: The opening refrain returns between changing episodes. Birds, streams and a storm belong to the accompanying sonnet, not to a story invented by later listeners; Vivaldi links its images to the musical score.
question: How does a returning refrain hold the changing scenes together?

relations.label: The ritornello closes the movement
relations.basis: The closing orchestral ritornello recalls the later phrases of the E-major opening refrain. The measured pair agrees with the closing section near 194 s; it does not imply that every bar of the first ritornello returns. CENS diagonal mean 0.965, sustained 14.5 s, fixed pitch-class shift 0 semitones and time offset 175.5 s (cache/form/vivaldi-spring-allegro.txt, candidate 1; 0.5 s grid). These are matched excerpts, not complete section boundaries; timing has not been checked by ear.

cues.title: A refrain to remember
cues.text: Remember the shape of the opening phrases. This is the ritornello, or returning refrain: material that links the episodes, sometimes coming back in a shortened form rather than as a complete repeat.
cues.evidence: The University of North Georgia’s Resonances chapter explains the opening refrain and its shortened returns. This cue concerns the movement’s design, not a timed instrumental entrance: https://human.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Music/Ethnomusicology/Resonances_-_Engaging_Music_in_its_Cultural_Context_(Morgan-Ellis_Ed.)/02%3A_Music_for_Storytelling/06%3A_Stories_without_Words/6.04%3A_Antonio_Vivaldi_-_The_Four_Seasons_Spring
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Calls instead of a single line
cues.text: The first episode represents the sonnet’s birds greeting spring. Listen for short figures that seem to answer one another, rather than trying to join everything into one uninterrupted melody.
cues.evidence: Resonances places the birdsong episode after the opening refrain. The recording’s change of activity around 0:34 helps estimate the region, but no particular bird-call figure has been aligned: https://human.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Music/Ethnomusicology/Resonances_-_Engaging_Music_in_its_Cultural_Context_(Morgan-Ellis_Ed.)/02%3A_Music_for_Storytelling/06%3A_Stories_without_Words/6.04%3A_Antonio_Vivaldi_-_The_Four_Seasons_Spring
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The Pietà’s violin teacher
cues.text: Vivaldi became violin teacher at Venice’s Ospedale della Pietà in 1703, the year he was ordained a priest. Teaching and instrumental composition were central parts of his work there.
cues.evidence: The Church of the Pietà’s biography records the ordination and violin-teaching appointment in 1703 and describes his teaching and composing: https://www.vivaldichurchvenice.com/en/biography-of-antonio-vivaldi

cues.title: A poem beside the parts
cues.text: The Four Seasons appeared in the 1725 collection Il cimento dell’armonia e dell’inventione. Each concerto had a sonnet, linked by letters to passages in the score. No author was named for the poems; attribution to Vivaldi remains an inference.
cues.evidence: Resonances describes the 1725 publication, the lettered connections between sonnets and score, and the absence of an author’s name: https://human.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Music/Ethnomusicology/Resonances_-_Engaging_Music_in_its_Cultural_Context_(Morgan-Ellis_Ed.)/02%3A_Music_for_Storytelling/06%3A_Stories_without_Words/6.04%3A_Antonio_Vivaldi_-_The_Four_Seasons_Spring

cues.title: A storm within the form
cues.text: The score’s storm episode uses rapid figures and repeated notes before the birds return. Listen for how this unsettled scene changes the character without removing the refrain that holds the movement together.
cues.evidence: The score commentary connects rapid writing with the sonnet’s thunderstorm and describes the following return of birdsong. Placement in this recording is provisional; an audio-feature change around 1:55 is not an identified lightning entrance: https://human.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Music/Ethnomusicology/Resonances_-_Engaging_Music_in_its_Cultural_Context_(Morgan-Ellis_Ed.)/02%3A_Music_for_Storytelling/06%3A_Stories_without_Words/6.04%3A_Antonio_Vivaldi_-_The_Four_Seasons_Spring
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Recognising a fragment
cues.text: Listen for a small part of the opening refrain rather than waiting for its complete return. How little of a familiar phrase is needed before you recognise it?
cues.evidence: The movement uses abbreviated returns of its refrain. This is a recognition prompt across the later episodes, not a claim that a specific fragment starts at this second.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Activity and arrival
cues.text: Compare the mobile figures with the more settled shape of the refrain. Does the sense of arrival come from slowing the activity, recognising the phrase, or both?
cues.evidence: The prompt concerns the documented alternation of refrain and episodes. The feature report alone cannot establish the exact return of a theme or home key.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: A compact return to finish
cues.text: The final refrain closes the movement without retelling every scene. Compare its familiar shape with the opening, then follow the last phrase into the remaining resonance.
cues.evidence: Resonances identifies a shortened refrain as the conclusion. The reduced attacks and level in the recording’s final stretch support this approximate placement, not an exact final-chord timestamp: https://human.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Music/Ethnomusicology/Resonances_-_Engaging_Music_in_its_Cultural_Context_(Morgan-Ellis_Ed.)/02%3A_Music_for_Storytelling/06%3A_Stories_without_Words/6.04%3A_Antonio_Vivaldi_-_The_Four_Seasons_Spring
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: A cadence opens space for three birds
transitions.how: The refrain closes in E major, its dominant B resolving to E, before the solo violin and two orchestral violinists exchange birdsong figures. Trills and little ascending or descending shapes replace the tutti’s strongly grouped phrases. The key does not change: tonic and dominant pedals, E and B, hold the episode in the same harmonic field while the upper lines become independent. Vivaldi changes the number and spacing of the speaking voices rather than introducing a new tempo.
transitions.evidence: The 0:34 section boundary has an analysis change and increased brightness. José Rodríguez Alvira’s score analysis at https://www.teoria.com/en/articles/2021/vivaldi-seasons/primavera/01.php identifies bars 13–27 as E-major birdsong with tonic and dominant pedals, using this Harrison recording; Resonances identifies the three violinists. The passage boundary is retained rather than timing an individual trill.

transitions.title: The bass gathers the separate calls together
transitions.how: The separate bird calls give way to the strings moving together in the refrain’s second phrase. Vivaldi omits its opening phrase and the repeat: a small recognisable portion is enough. Repeated E notes in the bass underpin E-major chords alternating with A major over E, so the upper parts can move while the tonic remains fixed below. A B-to-E cadence completes the compact return, ready for the quieter running semiquavers of the stream episode.
transitions.evidence: The 1:08 section boundary lies between analysis changes at 1:04 and 1:12; level rises from roughly −23.1 dB at 1:05 to −12.8 dB at 1:10. Rodríguez Alvira’s displayed score of bars 27–30 shows the shortened second phrase, E bass pedal, A-major six-four chords and B–E cadence: https://www.teoria.com/en/articles/2021/vivaldi-seasons/primavera/01.php

transitions.title: The dominant-key refrain releases a storm
transitions.how: The preceding refrain has reached B major, E major’s dominant key. The storm replaces its measured phrases with repeated-note thunder, rising scales and the soloist’s rapid arpeggios. The bass is no longer simply the refrain’s repeated tonic: the harmony travels through major-key territory towards C♯ minor. That relative-minor destination is then confirmed by another shortened refrain. The familiar phrase, rather than a new storm theme, makes the changed key audible after the rush.
transitions.evidence: The 1:56 section boundary is an analysis change within the storm region, with C♯-minor-compatible pitch content later in the span. Rodríguez Alvira identifies the B-major refrain in bars 40–44, the storm’s B/E-major to C♯-minor route in bars 44–55 and the minor refrain in bars 55–59. Resonances supplies the thunder, scales and solo arpeggios; no lightning stroke is timed.

transitions.title: The returning phrase changes its destination
transitions.how: After the birds resume in C♯ minor, the returning refrain itself carries the music back to E major. Its bass moves C♯–F♯–B–E: C♯ minor gives way to F♯ minor seventh, B dominant seventh and E major. F♯ minor seventh belongs to both keys, acting as iv in C♯ minor and ii in E major. The recognisable rhythmic figure holds the phrase together while that descending-fifths route changes its harmonic destination; the full strings make the return more collective than the preceding calls.
transitions.evidence: The 2:46 section boundary has a strong analysis change near the shift from C♯-minor to E-major-compatible estimates. Rodríguez Alvira’s score of bars 66–70 explicitly shows the C♯-minor opening and modulation through F♯ minor seventh and B seventh to E major: https://www.teoria.com/en/articles/2021/vivaldi-seasons/primavera/01.php. The same-recording guide places this ritornello broadly around 2:44–2:56.

transitions.title: The last solo hands back the cadence
transitions.how: The last solo passage prepares the final E-major refrain without introducing another image from the sonnet. The full strings take over its closing phrase, not the whole opening ritornello, and the bass resumes the familiar cadential support beneath the grouped melody. Dominant B gives way to tonic E to finish. Keeping only the closing material lets Vivaldi settle the key decisively without replaying the birds, stream or storm; the Allegro pulse remains intact through the handover.
transitions.evidence: The 3:14 section boundary agrees with the form relation matching 3:13.5–3:28 to the opening’s later phrase at 0:18–0:32.5. Rodríguez Alvira’s same-recording guide places the final refrain near 3:13; Resonances identifies it as the repeated closing phrase rather than the complete opening. The score supplies E major and its final dominant–tonic close, not a key label inferred from the tail.

facts: Violin with his father Giovanni Battista, a violinist at St Mark’s, Venice
Violin teacher at the Ospedale della Pietà from 1703; maestro de’ concerti from 1716; theatre work in Venice and other cities
More than 500 concertos; operas, sacred vocal music, sonatas and chamber cantatas
composer.background:
Vivaldi was born in Venice, the son of a barber who became a professional violinist at St Mark’s. Giovanni Battista Vivaldi taught his son the violin and remained involved in his musical work. Antonio trained for the priesthood and was ordained in 1703, acquiring the nickname il prete rosso, the red priest, from his hair. He soon ceased regularly celebrating Mass, later explaining that a condition of tightness in the chest prevented him. He travelled extensively, taught and managed operatic productions.

In 1703 the Ospedale della Pietà appointed him violin teacher. The Pietà was a charitable institution that cared for abandoned children; its celebrated performing body consisted of girls and women whose training could continue into adult professional responsibility within the institution. Concerts and services attracted Venetian patrons and foreign visitors. Vivaldi’s employment was periodically renewed and sometimes interrupted, but the connection endured for decades. The players supplied a practical laboratory: a concerto could be written for a particular instrumental skill, tried in performance, and followed by another that changed the problem.
composer.epithet: A violinist and theatre composer who made the returning orchestral refrain organise a soloist’s changing keys, textures and physical risks.
